name: THE OAXACA WAKA WAKA BURGER (comes with oaxaca cheese)

recipe.history:
Oaxaca cheese — known locally as quesillo — is one of Mexico's most beloved and versatile fresh cheeses, with its origins rooted in the Sierra Juárez mountain towns of the state of Oaxaca in southern Mexico, most notably the village of Reyes Etla. The cheese is a pasta filata variety, meaning it is made by stretching and kneading fresh curds in hot water — a technique shared with Italian mozzarella and provolone, likely introduced to Mexico by Dominican friars in the sixteenth century who brought cheesemaking knowledge from the Italian peninsula. Over time, Oaxacan cheesemakers adapted the technique to local milk, local culture, and local taste, developing a cheese distinctly their own: formed into long ribbons wound into a ball, with a milky, buttery flavor, a gentle acidity, and an unrivaled melting quality. When heat is applied, quesillo melts into long, glossy, stretching threads — a quality called "hilado" — that has made it the definitive cheese for Oaxacan tlayudas, quesadillas, and memelas. The cheese carries deep cultural significance in Oaxaca, where it is sold fresh in markets by women who carry the wound balls in their aprons, and where it is considered as fundamental to the regional table as mole negro or chapulines.

Oaxacan ingredients began entering American culinary consciousness in earnest during the late 1980s and 1990s, when chefs like Rick Bayless, Diana Kennedy, and later a generation of Mexican-American chefs began introducing the complexity and diversity of regional Mexican cuisine to a broader American audience. Quesillo specifically became more widely available in U.S. markets as the Mexican immigrant community grew and as specialty food stores and Latin grocery chains expanded their fresh cheese offerings. By the 2010s, Oaxaca cheese had crossed fully into mainstream American cooking — appearing on restaurant menus as a melting cheese in burgers, pizzas, and grilled sandwiches, prized precisely for those long, theatrical pull-apart threads that satisfy something deep and primal in the act of eating. The burger application is a natural one: the cheese's mild, fresh dairy flavor and its exceptional melt character give it an affinity with seasoned beef that rivals any classic option.

I first encountered quesillo at a street market in Oaxaca City on a trip I took in my late twenties — a solo journey intended as a reset after a period of professional and personal turbulence. I bought a ball of the cheese from a woman near the Mercado Benito Juárez who wound it in front of me from a long ribbon into a tight, glistening sphere, and I ate strips of it as I walked, the cheese squeaking faintly against my teeth the way fresh curds do. That evening I ate tlayudas at a rooftop restaurant with a view of Santo Domingo church lit up like a wedding cake, and the quesillo was melted over the black bean paste in a golden, stretching canopy that I have been trying to reproduce ever since. The idea of putting it on a burger came to me years later, and the first time I tried it, with a charred beef patty and chipotle crema on a toasted bolillo-style roll, I felt a small electric recognition — like two things I loved had always been meant to meet.

There is a philosophy embedded in cooking a burger to medium rare that goes beyond temperature preference, and it becomes especially apparent with a burger built around fresh, mild Oaxaca cheese. At 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C), the beef retains its moisture and its fat remains liquid and distributed throughout the patty. The flavor of the beef itself — grassy, mineral, rich — is fully present and available to mingle with the mild dairy sweetness of the melted quesillo. Cook that patty to 160°F and the fat renders out, the proteins seize, and you are left with a dense puck whose flavor must be supplied almost entirely by its accompaniments. Medium rare is not bravado. It is the temperature at which beef is most completely and honestly itself, which is the only starting point from which good cooking can proceed.
ingredients: 3 cups bread flour, plus more for shaping
1 tbsp cornstarch dissolved in 1/4 cup cold water (for crust wash)
12 oz Oaxaca cheese (quesillo), pulled into wide ribbons
2 to 3 chipotle chiles in adobo, minced to a paste
2 ripe Hass avocados, halved and pitted
1 small jalapeño, finely minced (seeds removed for mild)
1 cup shredded green cabbage, lightly salted
instructions: 1. Make the bolillo-style buns: Dissolve the yeast and sugar in the warm water in the bowl of a stand mixer and let bloom 5 minutes. Add the bread flour, salt, and lard. Mix on low with the dough hook 2 minutes, then increase to medium and knead 10 minutes until smooth, slightly firm, and elastic. The dough should be stiffer than a typical brioche dough. Form into a ball, place in a lightly oiled bowl, cover with plastic wrap, and rise 1 hour until doubled.

2. Divide the dough into 4 equal pieces. Shape each piece into an oval log approximately 5 inches long by 3 inches wide, tapering the ends slightly to give a slight torpedo shape — classic bolillo form adapted for burger use. Place on a parchment-lined baking sheet seam-side down. Cover and proof 30 minutes.

3. Preheat the oven to 400°F (205°C) and place a small pan of water on the oven floor or lowest rack to create steam. Brush each bun with the cornstarch wash. Score a single deep slash down the center of each bun with a sharp knife or lame. Bake 18 to 22 minutes until the crust is golden and firm and the bun sounds hollow when tapped on the bottom. Cool completely on a wire rack.

4. Make the chipotle crema: Stir together the Mexican crema, minced chipotle chiles, adobo sauce, grated garlic, lime juice, and salt until fully combined. Taste and adjust heat and salt. Refrigerate until needed.

5. Make the avocado smash: Scoop the avocado flesh into a bowl. Add the lime juice, diced white onion, chopped cilantro, salt, and minced jalapeño. Mash with a fork to a rough, chunky texture — some pieces of avocado should remain intact. Taste and adjust salt and lime. Cover with plastic wrap pressed directly to the surface and refrigerate until assembly.

6. Prepare the Oaxaca cheese: Pull the quesillo by hand into wide, flat ribbons approximately 6 to 8 inches long and 2 inches wide. Loosely arrange each portion (about 3 oz) in a nest-like mound ready to drape over the cooking patties.

7. Combine the ancho chile powder, cumin, garlic powder, salt, and black pepper in a small bowl. Divide the ground beef into 4 equal portions (8 oz / 227g each). Gently form each into a patty approximately 4 inches wide and 3/4 inch thick. Press a shallow dimple in the center. Season both sides of each patty liberally with the spice blend just before cooking.

8. Heat a cast-iron skillet or heavy griddle over high heat until smoking. Cook the patties 3 to 4 minutes on the first side without pressing, until a deep dark crust forms. Flip once. Immediately pile the Oaxaca cheese ribbons generously over each patty, letting them cascade over the edges. Cover the pan with a tight lid or metal dome and add a splash of water to generate steam. Cook 2 to 3 minutes more until the internal temperature reaches 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) and the cheese is fully melted into long, glossy threads. Remove and rest on a wire rack 3 minutes.
9. Split the bolillo buns and toast the cut sides on the hot skillet for 1 to 2 minutes until lightly charred and crisp.

10. Assemble: Spread a generous layer of chipotle crema on both bun halves. On the bottom bun, spread the avocado smash. Top with the shredded salted cabbage, then 2 slices of tomato. Place the melted-cheese-topped patty over the tomato. Garnish with fresh cilantro leaves. Cap with the top bun. Serve immediately with lime wedges and pickled jalapeños on the side.
